lead: Ben Sira paints Wisdom as a mother and teacher who tests her children before she trusts them, and then shows them her secrets. In the Gospel John wants to stop a stranger who drives out demons in Jesus’ name, and Jesus will not allow it. Psalm 119 sings of the great peace of those who love God’s law. Both readings teach the same lesson: Wisdom, and the name of Jesus, are larger than the circle we draw around ourselves.

set: The Book of Sirach is the work of a Jerusalem teacher, Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach (50:27), written in Hebrew about 180 BC. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt some fifty years later, as his prologue tells. The Church received the book in Greek; large parts of the Hebrew were found again from 1896 onward, first in the Cairo Genizah and later at Masada and Qumran. Latin Christians called it Ecclesiasticus, the “church book”, because it was so widely used for teaching. It is one of the deuterocanonical books, received by the Catholic Church as Scripture.

In chapter 4 the teacher has just spoken of care for the poor and the orphan (4:1–10). Now he turns to Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman who brings up children, a figure he will develop at length in chapter 24.
str: vv. 11–13: Wisdom teaches and helps; those who love her are filled with joy.
vv. 14–16: to serve her is to serve the Holy One; the faithful inherit her.
vv. 17–18: first the hard road of her discipline, then gladness and her secrets.
v. 19: the warning: those who stray are left to their ruin.
kw: In Sirach wisdom is practical skill for living rightly before God, and also something greater: a gift that comes from the Lord (1:1) and is close to him, here pictured as a person.
Training, the bringing up of a child, with its corrections (v. 17). Ben Sira knows that learning costs something. Hebrews 12:5–11 uses the same word for the Lord’s discipline of his children.

“Those who serve her minister to the Holy One” (v. 14). In the Greek Old Testament this verb is used for the service of priests, and our word “liturgy” comes from it. To live wisely is itself a kind of worship.
vv: Wisdom teaches her children and gives help to those who seek her.
The NRSV follows the Hebrew, “teaches”. The Greek, which the Malayalam follows, says that Wisdom “exalts” her sons. Both are true of her: she instructs, and she lifts up.
Whoever loves her loves life, and those who seek her from early morning are filled with joy.
Seeking “from early morning” is the language of eager love (compare Proverbs 8:17). Wisdom is not a subject one studies once; she is sought every day.
For at first she will walk with them on tortuous paths;
An honest word. The road to wisdom has bends and trials. She tests before she trusts, and then she “will come straight back to them again and gladden them” (v. 18).
ch: Christians have long heard in these portraits of Wisdom an echo of Christ, whom Paul calls “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). The Catechism names wisdom first among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831). The road Ben Sira describes, discipline first and then joy, is the road of every disciple who keeps faith through dark times.

r.h: Whoever is not against us is for us
set: We are in the house at Capernaum (9:33). Jesus has just foretold his passion for the second time (9:31), and the disciples have argued on the road about who is the greatest. He has set a child among them and said that whoever welcomes such a child in his name welcomes him (9:37). The word “name” sets John speaking; this is the only place in Mark where John speaks on his own.

Background. Numbers 11:26–29 tells a similar story. Two elders, Eldad and Medad, prophesied in the camp although they had not gone out to the tent, and Joshua asked Moses to stop them. Moses answered that he wished all the Lord’s people were prophets.
str: v. 38: John reports that they tried to stop an outsider.
v. 39: Jesus says, do not stop him: no one who does a deed of power in my name will soon speak evil of me.
v. 40: the principle: whoever is not against us is for us.
kw: In the Bible the name stands for the person and his power. The man drives out demons “in your name”, by calling on Jesus himself. The word runs through these verses: in my name (v. 37), in your name (v. 38), in my name (v. 39).
“He was not following us,” says John, not “you”. The disciples measure by belonging to their group; Jesus measures by a person’s relation to himself.
Mark’s usual word for Jesus’ miracles. Even outside the circle of the Twelve, the power at work is his.
vv: Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.
Only a little earlier the disciples themselves could not drive out a demon (9:18, 28). The man they want to stop is doing what they had failed to do.
Jesus is not jealous for the size of his group but glad for the good done in his name.
Whoever is not against us is for us.

In Matthew 12:30 Jesus says, “Whoever is not with me is against me.” The sayings do not contradict each other. One warns our own hearts: no one can stay neutral before Jesus. The other teaches generosity toward others who do good in his name.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the one Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, while many elements of sanctification and of truth are found outside her visible structure (Lumen Gentium 8). Catholics are asked to acknowledge gladly the truly Christian gifts found among other Christians (Unitatis Redintegratio 4). The disciple rejoices wherever the name of Jesus brings healing, and does not confuse loyalty to Christ with suspicion of everyone outside one’s own circle.

qa: Does this mean it does not matter which Church one belongs to?

No. Jesus is not saying that every group is the same, but that good done in his name comes from him and must not be opposed out of rivalry. The Church teaches that the fullness of the means of salvation is found in the Catholic Church (Unitatis Redintegratio 3). At the same time she honours what is truly of Christ in other Christians, and prays and works for unity.
study: Where do I find it hard to rejoice in good done by people outside my own group or parish?
Ben Sira says Wisdom tests before she trusts. What hard stretch of my road might be her discipline?
